text: The chief justice of Kenya is a public office established under Article 161 of the country's Constitution as the head of the Judiciary of Kenya and, under Article 163, also serves as the president of the Supreme Court of Kenya. The chief justice is assisted by the deputy chief justice, who also serves as the deputy president of the Supreme Court. The current chief justice is Lady Justice Martha Koome, the first woman to hold this position. Prior to the 2010 Constitution, the president appointed the chief justice without interview or parliamentary approval and could dismiss them at will. Under the new Constitution, the chief justice is appointed by the president but selected by the Judicial Service Commission through a competitive process involving a vacancy announcement, shortlisting, and interviews. To qualify, a candidate must have at least fifteen years of experience as a legal practitioner. After interviews, the Judicial Service Commission selects one individual whose name is sent to Parliament for vetting and approval; if Parliament approves, the president formally appoints the candidate. The Jubilee Coalition, while in power, introduced a legislative amendment requiring the Judicial Service Commission to submit three qualified candidates for the president to choose from, but the constitutional court declared this amendment unconstitutional, and the original appointment process remains the only legal method. Like other judges, the chief justice serves until age 70, with the option of early retirement at 65, but may not serve more than ten years in the role—after ten years, they must retire even if under 70, though they may continue as an associate justice until age 70. The chief justice may be removed if a tribunal finds they are no longer fit for office. In the event of a vacancy, the deputy chief justice acts until a new chief justice is appointed; if the deputy position is also vacant, the senior-most associate justice of the Supreme Court acts as president, and the next senior-most as deputy president—this occurred in 2016 when Associate Justice Mohamed Ibrahim served as president following the early retirement of Chief Justice Willy Mutunga (who turned 69 in June 2016) and Deputy Chief Justice Kalpana Rawal (who turned 70 in January 2016). The chief justice performs judicial, administrative, and ceremonial duties as provided by the Constitution and statutes, including presiding over the Supreme Court, directing which associate justices preside over cases, leading the Judicial Service Commission in setting judicial policies and recruiting judges and magistrates, and serving as the administrative head of the judiciary—though the chief registrar oversees administrative matters. The chief justice also presides over the swearing-in of the president, deputy president, and other government officials and ceremonially administers the oath of admission to the Roll of Advocates. The office of Deputy Chief Justice was created for the first time under the 2010 Constitution.
